transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-08
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Raman (Redwood); Aisha Khan, Marcus Vale, Diego Alvarez (Pioneer Diagnostics)

Summary (auto): quick alignment on p95 definition and the metrics we need to collect; agreed to run a small sandbox benchmark on 8k-context model and to share capacity planning doc.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:02] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we got about 50 minutes, does that still work?
[00:00:10] Aisha Khan: Yep that's fine, thanks. We wanted to focus on latency tails and throughput numbers, especially p95 and peak tokens per second.
[00:00:18] Marcus Vale: And to be clear, we're evaluating hosted first but we might need dedicated or private for PHI later, so curious about the trade-offs.
[00:00:25] Jordan Lee: Totally, that's common. Priya will jump into the technical detail, Priya you good?
[00:00:29] Priya Raman: Yep, hi all. Quick agenda: align on p95 definition, traffic profile, streaming vs non-streaming, then propose bench plan.
[00:00:36] Diego Alvarez: Quick note, our current proto runs on in-house GPUs but the ops team is strained--we want something we can operate without rewriting infra.
[00:00:42] Jordan Lee: Understood. So first, p95: do you have a SLO number in mind?
[00:00:48] Aisha Khan: We're aiming for under 300ms p95 for short prompts (~80-120 tokens) in interactive flows, and under 800ms p95 for longer streaming generative responses (2-3k tokens).
[00:00:58] Priya Raman: Ok, that's helpful. Is the shorter prompt path strict user-facing UI latency or background?
[00:01:04] Aisha Khan: UI, user-facing. It's a chat assistant inside our clinician dashboard.
[00:01:08] Marcus Vale: And our concurrency target is about 150 concurrent users during peak, with a burst multiplier up to 3x for short windows. Avg tokens per request is 90-110, peaks with streaming could hit 2.5k tokens for a few requests.
[00:01:22] Priya Raman: Good numbers. For Hosted mode we have published p95 numbers for our curated models but real workload shape matters—sequence length distribution, tokenization variance etc.
[00:01:32] Diego Alvarez: How do you handle KV cache and prefix caching? We have a lot of repeated prefixes in templates.
[00:01:37] Priya Raman: We do prefix / KV caching at the routing layer; that can dramatically reduce per-token cost and improve tail latency for repeated contexts. But it depends on your cache hit rate.
[00:01:45] Marcus Vale: Our templates would likely hit cache 60-70% of the time for the first hundred tokens.
[00:01:50] Jordan Lee: Good, that helps sizing. Two important distinctions: hosted gives fastest onboarding and transparent numbers, Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity and more predictable p95 under burst, Private gives full network control and KMS but requires more ops.
[00:02:05] Aisha Khan: For private, our security team will want evidence of SOC2 and KMS integration. We also need audit logs for prompt retention policies.
[00:02:12] Jordan Lee: We can share security docs; Redwood Private supports KMS integration and audit logs — we'll send SOC2 and the redacted compliance pack.
[00:02:20] Marcus Vale: Cool. Let's talk benchmarks.
[00:02:23] Priya Raman: Proposed benchmark approach: 1) small synthetic load to measure per-request latency distribution across sequence lengths; 2) ramp tests for concurrency; 3) streaming tail tests to measure p95 and p99 token emission latency; 4) token/sec end-to-end throughput tests.
[00:02:39] Diego Alvarez: For streaming tail tests, do you measure per-token latency or chunk latency?
[00:02:43] Priya Raman: We measure both actually. Per-token latency is noisy but important; we also report chunk-latency which is more meaningful for user-visible streaming gaps.
[00:02:50] Aisha Khan: Example: clinicians see typing indicator; we don't want >300ms gaps between token chunks or they think the system hung.
[00:02:56] Jordan Lee: Right. Also worth calling out cold-starts — if model isn't warmed KV cache can add a few hundred ms, especially for large context.
[00:03:04] Marcus Vale: How does Redwood handle fallbacks in hosted mode when a node is overloaded? Do you route to a smaller quantized model?
[00:03:10] Priya Raman: Yes, smart routing can fallback to a compatible model variant — quantized or smaller architecture. That helps preserve availability while keeping a reasonable quality baseline.
[00:03:18] Diego Alvarez: Any examples of token/sec numbers for a 8k context LLM on hosted vs dedicated? Ballpark is fine.
[00:03:25] Priya Raman: Rough ballpark: on our hosted tiers for 8k context, single GPU inference for streaming might sustain 150-300 tokens/sec depending on batch and kernel perf; Dedicated with reserved multi-GPU or optimized kernels can push the effective system-wide tokens/sec much higher because of parallelism and batching. But exact depends on model family and quantization.
[00:03:44] Marcus Vale: Hmm 150-300 tokens/sec per GPU, if we have concurrency of 150 users at avg 100 tokens each that's a lot. Need to map RPS to GPU count.
[00:03:53] Jordan Lee: We'll provide a capacity calculator. For rough math: if each request streams 100 tokens over 2s, that's 50 tokens/sec per user during streaming; 150 concurrent users -> 7.5k tokens/sec aggregate. If each GPU does 250 tokens/sec, you'd need ~30 GPUs — but batching and concurrency multiplexing reduce that.
[00:04:13] Aisha Khan: That 30 GPUs number scares execs — we need to show realistic optimizations like batching, prefix caching, and fallbacks.
[00:04:20] Priya Raman: Exactly. Also can trade off model size or precision (quantization) for big improvements. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles that reduce per-token compute.
[00:04:29] Diego Alvarez: For the bench, can Redwood run the test in our cloud account or do we run it and share logs?
[00:04:34] Jordan Lee: Two options: we can run a quick hosted sandbox on our side with synthetic traffic or we can provide a benchmark harness script for you to run in your environment; for private deployments we'd coordinate with your infra team.
[00:04:44] Marcus Vale: We'd prefer running in our infra for Private evaluation, but for initial numbers hosted sandbox is fine. We'll do both eventually.
[00:04:51] Priya Raman: Ok, plan: hosted sandbox for immediate numbers, then a short dedicated pilot in your account for deeper profiling.
[00:04:58] Aisha Khan: One more: how do you instrument latency per request? Our SRE wants tracing to tie tokens back to request IDs.
[00:05:05] Priya Raman: We emit per-request traces and token metrics; we can integrate with your tracing (jaeger/zipkin/OpenTelemetry) and provide per-route dashboards in the Console.
[00:05:13] Diego Alvarez: Do you expose kernel-level telemetry — like GPU utilization per request?
[00:05:18] Priya Raman: We provide GPU util, batch sizes, kv cache hit rates, queue times. Kernel-level specifics are abstracted but we will share the relevant throughput and latency metrics.
[00:05:26] Jordan Lee: Quick note — when we quote p95 numbers we need to know whether customers are measuring end-to-end (client->client) or server-side generation only. Are you using client-side rendering times in your SLO?
[00:05:36] Marcus Vale: We'll measure end-to-end, but we can provide server-only logs for benchmarking.
[00:05:40] Priya Raman: Good. For the benchmark harness we'll ask for both: a synthetic client measuring end-to-end and server telemetry for isolating model time.
[00:05:47] Aisha Khan: Security constraints: our VPC peering rules are strict and we need to ensure no internet egress for PHI. For hosted we could use a dedicated tenancy with strict routing?
[00:05:56] Jordan Lee: Hosted can't be fully air-gapped; for PHI we usually recommend Dedicated or Private. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity inside cloud with private networking options; Private is the full VPC/on-prem option.
[00:06:06] Diego Alvarez: Any difference in p95 variance between hosted and dedicated?
[00:06:10] Priya Raman: Hosted has more multi-tenant variance but we mitigate with autoscaling and smart routing. Dedicated gives tighter variance because of reserved GPUs and predictable queues.
[00:06:18] Marcus Vale: Ok let's look at a concrete example — say 200 concurrent users, avg 100 tokens, p95 target 300ms for short prompts. What configuration would you recommend?
[00:06:28] Priya Raman: Quick sketch: If short prompts are the majority, you can optimize with a smaller, faster model variant for that route, colocate KV cache warmed units, and tune batching to favor low latency (smaller batch windows). That tends to need more instances but offers lower tail latency. For strict p95 300ms you'd likely want dedicated nodes to avoid noisy neighbors.
[00:06:46] Aisha Khan: Do you have recommendations on sequence-length aware routing?
[00:06:49] Priya Raman: Yes, route short prompts to a low-latency pool, long-form streaming to a high-throughput pool; automatic routing by policy is supported in the Console.
[00:06:57] Diego Alvarez: About the benchmark script, what languages and tooling? We use k6 for load and a python harness for streaming.
[00:07:03] Priya Raman: We have sample scripts in python and node for streaming and k6 for RPS probes. We'll share the harness repo link.
[00:07:09] Marcus Vale: Good. Can you also show an example of how batching delays are set? For interactive UI we want batch latency cap of 50ms.
[00:07:16] Priya Raman: Batching is tunable: you can set max batch latency and max batch size. We can suggest sensible defaults; but at 50ms cap you'll get smaller batches so throughput per GPU drops, hence more GPUs needed.
[00:07:27] Aisha Khan: Pricing question — if we go dedicated with 30 GPUs that sounds expensive; what are options?
[00:07:32] Jordan Lee: You can mix: dedicated for the critical low-latency pool and hosted for bulk non-critical traffic, also use quantized variants for cost savings. Optimize will propose a mix.
[00:07:40] Diego Alvarez: Any notes on failover? If a dedicated pool goes down, can traffic shift to hosted?
[00:07:45] Priya Raman: Yes, automatic fallback policies are supported — you can failover to hosted or a different region/model.
[00:07:51] Marcus Vale: Ok. For the immediate next step, we'd like the hosted sandbox numbers: p95 for 80-120 token prompts, streaming p95 for 2-3k tokens, plus token/sec throughput for a 1-minute sustained burst of our sample profile.
[00:08:02] Jordan Lee: We'll deliver that. Priya will own the sandbox run.
[00:08:06] Priya Raman: I'll need your sample distribution CSV and we can seed the sandbox with your templates to exercise prefix caching.
[00:08:12] Marcus Vale: I'll upload that. We'll also give you the SSO contact for our security team.
[00:08:17] Jordan Lee: Great. Anything else before we wrap?
[00:08:20] Aisha Khan: One small ask — can you include example Console dashboards and the traces format? Our SRE wants a preview.
[00:08:26] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll share screenshots and a sample OpenTelemetry trace export.
[00:08:31] Diego Alvarez: Also, how long does a Dedicated setup take? If we wanted to move next month.
[00:08:35] Jordan Lee: Provisioning dedicated capacity depends on region and GPU availability; for standard configs we can do weeks, for custom we might need longer. We'll put tentative timelines in the follow-up doc.
[00:08:44] Marcus Vale: Cool. I think that's it. Thanks everyone.
[00:08:47] Jordan Lee: Thanks, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and security docs.

--- End of main discussion; rest were quick confirmations ---
[00:32:10] (segment skipped in export)
[00:40:05] Priya Raman: Note: when we run the streaming test we'll capture per-chunk send times, queue sizes, kernel batch sizes, and GPU util.
[00:44:22] Marcus Vale: We'll also try a check with our heuristics that sometimes chop tokens to keep latency — want to see how that impacts qualitative outputs.
[00:47:11] Jordan Lee: Noted.
[00:51:30] Aisha Khan: Thanks, looking forward to the bench results.
